cards.q: Define proton number and nucleon number.
cards.a: Proton number (atomic number, Z\displaystyle ZZ): the number of protons in the nucleus. Nucleon number (mass number, A\displaystyle AA): the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

cards.q: A nucleus is written 614C\displaystyle {}^{14}_{6}\text{C}614​C. How many protons and how many neutrons does it contain?
cards.a: 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
cards.why: The lower number is the proton number. Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 14 − 6.

cards.q: What are isotopes?
cards.a: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

cards.q: Define the specific charge of a particle, and state its unit.
cards.a: Its charge divided by its mass. Unit: C kg−1\displaystyle \text{C kg}^{-1}C kg−1.

cards.a: 9.6×107 C kg−1\displaystyle 9.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}9.6×107 C kg−1
steps: specific charge=Qm=1.60×10−191.67×10−27\displaystyle \text{specific charge} = \frac{Q}{m} = \frac{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}}specific charge=mQ​=1.67×10−271.60×10−19​
=9.6×107 C kg−1\displaystyle = 9.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}=9.6×107 C kg−1

cards.a: 4.8×107 C kg−1\displaystyle 4.8 \times 10^{7}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}4.8×107 C kg−1
cards.why: Charge comes from the protons only; mass comes from all the nucleons.

cards.q: When finding the specific charge of an ion, what charge and what mass should be used?
cards.a: The net charge of the ion: the number of electrons gained or lost, times e\displaystyle ee. The mass of the whole ion, which is very nearly the mass of its nucleons.
cards.why: An uncharged atom has a specific charge of zero.

cards.q: What is the role of the strong nuclear force in a nucleus?
cards.a: It holds the nucleons together, overcoming the electrostatic repulsion between the protons, and so keeps the nucleus stable.

cards.q: Describe how the strong nuclear force between two nucleons depends on their separation.
cards.a: Repulsive at very short range, below about 0.5 fm. Attractive from there up to about 3 fm. Beyond about 3 fm it falls rapidly to zero.
cards.why: The repulsion at very short range stops the nucleus collapsing.

cards.q: In alpha decay, how do the nucleon number and the proton number of the nucleus change?
cards.a: The nucleon number falls by 4 and the proton number falls by 2.
cards.why: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

cards.q: Write the equation for the decay of a neutron in β−\displaystyle \beta^{-}β− decay.
cards.a: n→p+e−+νˉe\displaystyle \text{n} \rightarrow \text{p} + \text{e}^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}n→p+e−+νˉe​
cards.why: The nucleon number is unchanged and the proton number rises by 1. The antineutrino is needed to conserve lepton number.

cards.q: Why was the existence of the neutrino first proposed?
cards.a: To account for conservation of energy in beta decay. The beta particles were emitted with a range of energies, so another particle had to be carrying away the rest.

cards.q: How do the properties of an antiparticle compare with those of its particle?
cards.a: The same mass and rest energy, but opposite charge (and opposite baryon number, lepton number and strangeness).

cards.q: Name the antiparticles of the electron, the proton, the neutron and the neutrino.
cards.a: The positron, the antiproton, the antineutron and the antineutrino.

cards.q: What happens in annihilation?
cards.a: A particle meets its antiparticle and their mass is converted into energy, carried away by two photons.
cards.why: Two photons moving in opposite directions are needed to conserve momentum.

cards.q: What is pair production, and what is the minimum photon energy needed for it?
cards.a: A photon's energy is converted into a particle and its antiparticle. The photon needs at least twice the rest energy of the particle.

cards.q: The rest energy of an electron is 0.511 MeV. Calculate the minimum photon energy needed to produce an electron–positron pair.
cards.a: 1.02 MeV
steps: Both particles must be created, each with rest energy 0.511 MeV.
Emin=2×0.511\displaystyle E_{\text{min}} = 2 \times 0.511Emin​=2×0.511
Emin=1.02 MeV\displaystyle E_{\text{min}} = 1.02\ \text{MeV}Emin​=1.02 MeV

cards.q: Name the four fundamental interactions.
cards.a: Gravity, the electromagnetic interaction, the weak nuclear interaction and the strong nuclear interaction.

cards.q: How does the exchange particle model explain the force between two particles?
cards.a: The particles exchange a virtual particle, which carries momentum and energy between them. This exchange is the force.

cards.q: What is the exchange particle of the electromagnetic force?
cards.a: The virtual photon.

cards.q: What are the exchange particles of the weak interaction?
cards.a: The W+\displaystyle \text{W}^{+}W+ and W−\displaystyle \text{W}^{-}W− bosons.

cards.q: Which particles feel the strong interaction, and which feel the weak interaction?
cards.a: The strong interaction acts only on hadrons. The weak interaction acts on both hadrons and leptons.

cards.q: Describe β−\displaystyle \beta^{-}β− decay in terms of the exchange particle involved.
cards.a: A neutron changes into a proton and emits a W−\displaystyle \text{W}^{-}W−. The W−\displaystyle \text{W}^{-}W− then decays into an electron and an antineutrino.
cards.why: The W−\displaystyle \text{W}^{-}W− carries away negative charge, so the neutral neutron becomes a positive proton.

cards.q: Write the equation for β+\displaystyle \beta^{+}β+ decay of a proton, and name the exchange particle.
cards.a: p→n+e++νe\displaystyle \text{p} \rightarrow \text{n} + \text{e}^{+} + \nu_{e}p→n+e++νe​. The exchange particle is the W+\displaystyle \text{W}^{+}W+.

cards.q: Write the equation for electron capture.
cards.a: p+e−→n+νe\displaystyle \text{p} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{n} + \nu_{e}p+e−→n+νe​
cards.why: A proton in the nucleus captures an inner electron. The exchange particle is a W+\displaystyle \text{W}^{+}W+, from the proton to the electron.

cards.q: Electron capture and an electron–proton collision have the same overall equation. How do their exchange particles differ?
cards.a: In electron capture a W+\displaystyle \text{W}^{+}W+ passes from the proton to the electron. In an electron–proton collision a W−\displaystyle \text{W}^{-}W− passes from the electron to the proton.

cards.q: What is a hadron, and what are the two classes of hadron?
cards.a: A particle that feels the strong interaction; hadrons are made of quarks. The two classes are baryons and mesons.

cards.q: What is a baryon made of? Give two examples.
cards.a: Three quarks. Examples: the proton and the neutron.

cards.q: What is a meson made of? Give an example.
cards.a: A quark and an antiquark. Example: the pion.

cards.q: What is a lepton? Give two examples.
cards.a: A fundamental particle that does not feel the strong interaction. Examples: the electron and the neutrino.

cards.q: What are the baryon numbers of a baryon, an antibaryon, a meson and a lepton?
cards.a: Baryon: +1. Antibaryon: −1. Mesons and leptons: 0.

cards.q: Which is the only stable baryon?
cards.a: The proton. Other baryons eventually decay into it.

cards.q: Which particle is the exchange particle of the strong nuclear force between nucleons?
cards.a: The pion.

cards.q: What does a kaon decay into, and what does a muon decay into?
cards.a: A kaon decays into pions. A muon decays into an electron (with neutrinos).

cards.q: How is lepton number conserved in an interaction involving both electrons and muons?
cards.a: Separately for each type: the electron lepton number and the muon lepton number must each be the same before and after.
cards.why: Leptons have lepton number +1, antileptons −1, and all other particles 0.

cards.q: What are strange particles?
cards.a: Particles that are produced through the strong interaction but decay through the weak interaction, such as kaons. They are always created in pairs.

cards.q: When is strangeness conserved, and when can it change?
cards.a: It is conserved in strong interactions. In weak interactions it can change by 0, +1 or −1.

cards.q: In an interaction the strangeness changes by 1. A student says it must be a strong interaction because strange particles are involved. Correct this.
cards.a: It must be a weak interaction. Strangeness is always conserved in strong interactions; only the weak interaction can change it.

cards.q: State the charges of the up, down and strange quarks, in units of e\displaystyle ee.
cards.a: Up: +23\displaystyle +\frac{2}{3}+32​. Down: −13\displaystyle -\frac{1}{3}−31​. Strange: −13\displaystyle -\frac{1}{3}−31​.
cards.why: Each has baryon number +13\displaystyle +\frac{1}{3}+31​. Only the strange quark has strangeness, −1\displaystyle -1−1.

cards.q: State the quark composition of a proton and of a neutron.
cards.a: Proton: uud. Neutron: udd.
cards.why: Check the charges: 23+23−13=+1\displaystyle \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = +132​+32​−31​=+1, and 23−13−13=0\displaystyle \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = 032​−31​−31​=0.

cards.q: State the quark composition of an antiproton and of an antineutron.
cards.a: Antiproton: uˉ uˉ dˉ\displaystyle \bar{u}\,\bar{u}\,\bar{d}uˉuˉdˉ. Antineutron: uˉ dˉ dˉ\displaystyle \bar{u}\,\bar{d}\,\bar{d}uˉdˉdˉ.
cards.why: Replace every quark with its antiquark.

cards.q: State the quark compositions of the π+\displaystyle \pi^{+}π+ and the π−\displaystyle \pi^{-}π−.
cards.a: π+\displaystyle \pi^{+}π+: udˉ\displaystyle u\bar{d}udˉ. π−\displaystyle \pi^{-}π−: duˉ\displaystyle d\bar{u}duˉ.
cards.why: Check the charge of the π+\displaystyle \pi^{+}π+: +23+13=+1\displaystyle +\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} = +1+32​+31​=+1. The π0\displaystyle \pi^{0}π0 is uuˉ\displaystyle u\bar{u}uuˉ or ddˉ\displaystyle d\bar{d}ddˉ.

cards.q: State the quark compositions of the K+\displaystyle \text{K}^{+}K+, the K0\displaystyle \text{K}^{0}K0 and the K−\displaystyle \text{K}^{-}K−.
cards.a: K+\displaystyle \text{K}^{+}K+: usˉ\displaystyle u\bar{s}usˉ. K0\displaystyle \text{K}^{0}K0: dsˉ\displaystyle d\bar{s}dsˉ. K−\displaystyle \text{K}^{-}K−: suˉ\displaystyle s\bar{u}suˉ.
cards.why: Every kaon contains a strange quark or antiquark, which is what makes it a strange particle.

cards.q: What change of quark takes place in β−\displaystyle \beta^{-}β− decay, and in β+\displaystyle \beta^{+}β+ decay?
cards.a: β−\displaystyle \beta^{-}β−: a down quark changes to an up quark. β+\displaystyle \beta^{+}β+: an up quark changes to a down quark.
cards.why: In β−\displaystyle \beta^{-}β− decay a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud).

cards.q: Which quantities are always conserved in a particle interaction?
cards.a: Charge, baryon number and lepton number, together with energy and momentum.

cards.q: Use conservation laws to decide whether n→p+e−+νe\displaystyle \text{n} \rightarrow \text{p} + \text{e}^{-} + \nu_{e}n→p+e−+νe​ is possible.
cards.a: Not possible: lepton number is not conserved.
cards.why: With an antineutrino in place of the neutrino the lepton numbers are +1 and −1, and the decay is allowed.
steps: Charge: 0→+1−1+0=0\displaystyle 0 \rightarrow +1 - 1 + 0 = 00→+1−1+0=0. Conserved.
Baryon number: 1→1+0+0=1\displaystyle 1 \rightarrow 1 + 0 + 0 = 11→1+0+0=1. Conserved.
Lepton number: 0→0+1+1=2\displaystyle 0 \rightarrow 0 + 1 + 1 = 20→0+1+1=2. Not conserved, so the interaction cannot happen.

cards.q: Use conservation laws to decide whether p+p→p+p+π0\displaystyle \text{p} + \text{p} \rightarrow \text{p} + \text{p} + \pi^{0}p+p→p+p+π0 is possible.
cards.a: Possible: charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved (given enough kinetic energy to create the pion).
steps: Charge: 1+1→1+1+0\displaystyle 1 + 1 \rightarrow 1 + 1 + 01+1→1+1+0. Conserved.
Baryon number: 1+1→1+1+0\displaystyle 1 + 1 \rightarrow 1 + 1 + 01+1→1+1+0. Conserved.
Lepton number: 0→0\displaystyle 0 \rightarrow 00→0. Conserved.

cards.q: Explain how large-angle alpha particle scattering by gold foil gives evidence for the nuclear model of the atom.
cards.a: A very few alpha particles are turned through large angles, so the atom must contain a tiny, dense, charged centre.
marks: Most alpha particles pass straight through, so most of the atom is empty space.
A few are deflected through small angles, so there is charge concentrated in the atom that repels them.
A very small number are deflected through more than 90°, so that charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small region: the nucleus.

cards.q: What is thermionic emission?
cards.a: The release of electrons from the surface of a heated metal.
cards.why: Heating gives some electrons enough energy to escape. They can then be accelerated by an electric field.

cards.q: Explain how a linear accelerator (linac) accelerates charged particles.
cards.a: The particles gain energy from an electric field each time they cross a gap between tubes.
marks: The particles pass through a line of drift tubes connected to an alternating potential difference.
They are accelerated by the electric field in the gap between each pair of tubes.
Inside a tube there is no field, so they travel at constant speed.
The potential difference reverses while they are inside a tube, so the next gap also accelerates them.
The tubes get longer along the accelerator, so the faster particles still spend the same time in each.

cards.q: Explain how a cyclotron accelerates charged particles.
cards.a: A magnetic field bends the particles in semicircles, and an electric field accelerates them each time they cross a gap.
marks: Two hollow D-shaped electrodes (dees) sit in a uniform magnetic field, perpendicular to their plane.
The magnetic field makes the particles move in a circular path inside each dee.
An alternating potential difference between the dees accelerates the particles each time they cross the gap.
As they speed up, the radius of their path increases, so they spiral outwards.

cards.q: Derive the expression r=pBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{p}{BQ}r=BQp​ for the radius of the path of a charged particle moving at right angles to a magnetic field.
cards.a: r=pBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{p}{BQ}r=BQp​
steps: The magnetic force on the particle is BQv\displaystyle BQvBQv, at right angles to its velocity.
This force provides the centripetal force: BQv=mv2r\displaystyle BQv = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}BQv=rmv2​.
Rearrange: r=mvBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{mv}{BQ}r=BQmv​.
mv\displaystyle mvmv is the momentum p\displaystyle pp, so r=pBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{p}{BQ}r=BQp​.

cards.q: An electron moves at 2.0×107 m s−1\displaystyle 2.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}2.0×107 m s−1 at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 5.0×10−3 T\displaystyle 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{T}5.0×10−3 T. Calculate the radius of its path. (me=9.11×10−31 kg\displaystyle m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}me​=9.11×10−31 kg, e=1.60×10−19 C\displaystyle e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}e=1.60×10−19 C)
cards.a: 0.023 m

r=pBQ=1.82×10−235.0×10−3×1.60×10−19\displaystyle r = \frac{p}{BQ} = \frac{1.82 \times 10^{-23}}{5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}}r=BQp​=5.0×10−3×1.60×10−191.82×10−23​
r=0.023 m\displaystyle r = 0.023\ \text{m}r=0.023 m

cards.q: What can be deduced from the track of a particle in a detector placed in a magnetic field?
cards.a: Only charged particles leave tracks, because they ionise. The direction of curvature gives the sign of the charge. The radius gives the momentum: a tighter curve means a smaller momentum.
cards.why: A track that spirals inwards shows a particle losing energy.

cards.q: Why are very high energies needed to investigate the structure of nucleons?
cards.a: To resolve detail inside a nucleon, the particle used as a probe must have a de Broglie wavelength about as small as that detail. A shorter wavelength needs a larger momentum, so a very high energy.

cards.q: Give a situation in which the relativistic increase in a particle's lifetime is significant.
cards.a: When the particle moves at close to the speed of light. Fast-moving unstable particles, such as muons made in the upper atmosphere, are observed to live much longer than the same particles at rest, so they travel much further before decaying.

cards.q: Which quark was predicted by the symmetry of the standard quark–lepton model before it was observed?
cards.a: The top quark.
cards.why: The model has matching numbers of quarks and leptons, so a missing quark was expected.
